abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to train agents from pre-collected datasets. However, this comes with the added challenge of estimating the value of behaviors not covered in the dataset. Model-based methods offer a potential solution by training an approximate dynamics model, which then allows collection of additional synthetic data via rollouts in this model. The prevailing theory treats this approach as online RL in an approximate dynamics model, and any remaining performance gap is therefore understood as being due to dynamics model errors. In this paper, we analyze this assumption and investigate how popular algorithms perform as the learned dynamics model is improved. In contrast to both intuition and theory, if the learned dynamics model is replaced by the true error-free dynamics, existing model-based methods completely fail. This reveals a key oversight: The theoretical foundations assume sampling of full horizon rollouts in the learned dynamics model; however, in practice, the number of model-rollout steps is aggressively reduced to prevent accumulating errors. We show that this truncation of rollouts results in a set of edge-of-reach states at which we are effectively "bootstrapping from the void." This triggers pathological value overestimation and complete performance collapse. We term this the edge-of-reach problem. Based on this new insight, we fill important gaps in existing theory, and reveal how prior model-based methods are primarily addressing the edge-of-reach problem, rather than model-inaccuracy as claimed. Finally, we propose Reach-Aware Value Learning (RAVL), a simple and robust method that directly addresses the edge-of-reach problem and hence - unlike existing methods - does not fail as the dynamics model is improved. Since world models will inevitably improve, we believe this is a key step towards future-proofing offline RL.

# The Edge-of-Reach Problem in Offline Model-Based Reinforcement Learning Anya Sims† Cong Lu† Yee Whye Teh† # Abstract Offline reinforcement learning aims to enable agents to be trained from pre-collected datasets, however, this comes with the added challenge of estimating the value of behavior not covered in the dataset. Model-based methods offer a solution by allowing agents to collect additional synthetic data via rollouts in a learned dynamics model. The prevailing theoretical understanding is that this can then be viewed as online reinforcement learning in an approximate dynamics model, and any remaining gap is therefore assumed to be due to the imperfect dynamics model. Surprisingly, however, we find that if the learned dynamics model is replaced by the true error-free dynamics, existing model-based methods completely fail. This reveals a major misconception. Our subsequent investigation finds that the general procedure used in model-based algorithms results in the existence of a set of edge-of-reach states which trigger pathological value overestimation and collapse in Bellman-based algorithms. We term this the edge-of-reach problem. Based on this, we fill some gaps in existing theory and also explain how prior model-based methods are inadvertently addressing the true underlying edge-of-reach problem. Finally, we propose Reach-Aware Value Learning (RAVL), a simple and robust method that directly addresses the edge-of-reach problem and achieves strong performance across both proprioceptive and pixel-based benchmarks. # 1. Introduction Standard online reinforcement learning (RL) requires the collection of large amounts of on-policy data throughout training. This can be both costly and unsafe, and hence represents a barrier against applying RL in domains such as healthcare (Shiranthika et al., 2022; Tang & Wiens, 2021) or robotics (Ball et al., 2021; Chebotar et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2021), and also against scaling RL to more complex ![](images/dcd67da3485115813daf7d0b9149e43f6492ad4f63cf8e94791837a1a227745d.jpg) Figure 1: Boundaries of the states reachable at each timestep in the $k$ -step rollouts from $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{offline}}$ as used in offline model-based RL. In this paper we investigate a hitherto unrecognized pathology in offline model-based methods whereby edge-of-reach states - those only reachable at the final step of model rollouts (in red) - can trigger value overestimation and collapse of training. problems. Offline RL (Ernst et al., 2005; Levine et al., 2020) aims to remove this need for online data collection by enabling agents to be trained on pre-collected datasets. The use of large pre-existing datasets has driven significant recent advances in supervised learning (Brown et al., 2020), and one hope is that offline RL may provide a route for similar scaling in RL (Kumar et al., 2023). The central challenge in offline RL is dealing with value estimation for counterfactual actions not present in the dataset, termed the out-of-sample action problem (Kostrikov et al., 2022).1 A naive approach results in inaccurate values at out-of-sample state-action being propagated through the entire state-action space, leading to pathological training dynamics often exhibited as extreme value overestimation (Kumar et al., 2019). There have been many proposals to resolve this, with methods largely falling into one of two categories: model-free (An et al., 2021; Fujimoto & Gu, 2021; Fujimoto et al., 2019; Kostrikov et al., 2022; Kumar et al., 2019; 2020) or model-based (Kidambi et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2020). Model-free methods typically address this issue by applying a form of conservatism or constraint to avoid using out-of-sample actions in the Bellman update. In contrast, model-based methods, which are the focus of this paper, generally aim to resolve the issue by using the offline dataset to fit an approximate dynamics model (Janner et al., 2019; Sutton, 1991), and then allowing the agent to collect additional data in this learned dynamics model through fixed horizon rollouts from the original offline dataset (the general MBPO procedure (Janner et al., 2019), see Algorithm 1). The current understanding is that this converts the offline learning problem into online RL in an approximate dynamics model, thus solving the out-of-sample problem by allowing the agent to collect corrective feedback for any misestimated values. With this understanding, model-based methods typically attribute any remaining difficulties to errors in the learned dynamics model, and algorithms are subsequently motivated by avoiding exploitation of model errors using some notion of dynamics uncertainty. This understanding of model-based approaches naturally implies that reducing dynamics model errors should improve performance. However, we begin with a surprising demonstration that existing offline model-based methods completely fail when trained with the true error-free dynamics model (see Table 1 below). This exposes a significant misconception in the current understanding of model-based offline RL and prompts us to reevaluate our understanding of how prior methods work. On investigation, we find that the use of short rollouts in these algorithms (as opposed to full horizon trajectories as collected in online RL) causes a critical and previously unnoticed problem. More specifically, it leads to the existence of states which, under any policy, can only be reached in the final rollout step (see red in Figure 1). These edge-of-reach states appear in the training distribution as nextstates, and are hence used in Bellman updates, but even with the ability to collect unlimited additional data, the agent is never able to observe the outcome of actions from them. The result is pathological overestimation of values, similar to that seen in model-free methods. We term this the edge-of-reach problem. Thus, contrary to common understanding, the out-of-sample problem central in model-free methods is not resolved by a model-based approach. This edge-of-reach problem reveals strong connections between the two previously disjoint subfields of offline model-free and model-based RL. With this new understanding, we propose Reach-Aware Value Learning (RAVL), a robust scalable solution that takes an existing solution to the central out-of-sample problem in model-free literature, and directly applies it to the edge-of-reach problem in model-based methods (both proprioceptive and pixel-based). We first analyze RAVL on simple toy environments, and then show that it scales to the standard D4RL (Fu et al., 2020) and the V-D4RL (Lu et al., 2023) benchmarks. Furthermore, we anticipate that this unified understanding of model-based and model-free algorithms may pave the way for porting further strengths of existing model-free algorithms into model-based approaches. Code is open-sourced at: github.com/anyasims/edge-of-reach To summarize, our contributions are as follows: - We expose a significant misconception in the current understanding of offline model-based RL (Section 4.1). This leads to our hypothesis and definition of the edge-of-reach problem (Section 4.2). We provide evidence that this is the true underlying source of issues on the standard D4RL (Fu et al., 2020) benchmark (Section 4.4), before then constructing a simple environment which allows us to demonstrate and verify this hypothesis (Section 5). - Based on this, we propose Reach-Aware Value Learning (RAVL), a natural solution to the edge-of-reach problem (Section 6). We extensively evaluate RAVL across the D4RL and pixel-based V-D4RL (Lu et al., 2023) benchmarks (Section 7), including careful analysis into what RAVL is learning, demonstrating that it directly targets the edge-of-reach problem as intended (Section 7.1) and achieves state-of-the-art performance. - Finally, we give a more accurate explanation of the efficacy of prior methods, showing they unintentionally address the edge-of-reach problem (Section 7.4).2 # 2. Background Reinforcement Learning. We consider the standard RL framework (Sutton & Barto, 2018), in which the environment is formulated as a Markov Decision Process, $M = (\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, T, R, \mu_0, \gamma)$ , where $\mathcal{S}$ and $\mathcal{A}$ denote the state and action spaces, $T(s'|s, a)$ and $R(s, a)$ denote the transition and reward dynamics, $\mu_0$ the initial state distribution, and $\gamma \in (0,1)$ is the discount factor. The goal in reinforcement learning is to learn a policy $\pi(a|s)$ that maximizes the expected discounted return $\mathbb{E}_{\mu_0, \pi, T}[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t R(s_t, a_t)]$ . Actor-Critic Algorithms. The broad class of algorithms we consider are actor-critic (Konda & Tsitsiklis, 1999) methods which jointly optimize a policy $\pi$ and state-action value function ( $Q$ -function). Actor-critic algorithms iterate between fitting the $Q$ -function to the current policy (policy evaluation) and improving the policy relative to the $Q$ -function (policy improvement). The policy evaluation step relies on approximate dynamic programming with Bellman updates, updating the $Q$ -function using some dataset $\mathcal{D}$ as follows: $$ \begin{array}{l} Q ^ {j + 1} \leftarrow \underset {Q} {\arg \min } \mathbb {E} _ {(s, a, r, s ^ {\prime}) \sim \mathcal {D}, a ^ {\prime} \sim \pi^ {j} (\cdot | s ^ {\prime})} [ \\ \underbrace {\left(\underbrace {Q (s , a)} _ {\text {i n p u t}} - \underbrace {\left[ r + \gamma Q ^ {j} \left(s ^ {\prime} , a ^ {\prime}\right) \right]}\right) ^ {2} ]} _ {\text {B e l l m a n t a r g e t}} \tag {1} \\ \end{array} $$ Offline RL and the Out-of-Sample Problem. In online RL, the agent is able to collect new on-policy data throughout training. By contrast, in the offline setting, the algorithm has access only to a fixed offline dataset consisting of transition tuples $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{offline}} = \{(s,a,r,s')^{(i)}\}_{i = 1,\dots ,N}$ collected by Algorithm 1: Pseudocode for the base procedure used in offline model-based methods (MBPO, Janner et al. (2019)). In summary: (1) Train a dynamics model on $\mathcal{D}_{\text{offline}}$ , then (2) Train an agent (often SAC) with $k$ -step rollouts in the model starting from $s \in \mathcal{D}_{\text{offline}}$ . Existing methods consider issues to be due to model errors and hence introduce dynamics uncertainty penalties. We instead reveal that the true source of issues is the edge-of-reach problem, and propose a value pessimism approach to directly address this. some behavioral policies $\pi^{\beta}$ . The central problem in offline learning is the out-of-sample action problem: Target actions being sampled on-policy $a' \sim \pi^{j}$ means state-actions $(s', a')$ may not appear as $(s, a)$ in the dataset (see Equation (1)). Values at these out-of-sample state-actions are therefore never themselves updated and hence likely to be arbitrarily misestimated, but yet they are used for the targets in Bellman updates. Updates therefore propagate this misestimation to previous (in-sample) state-actions leading to a complete breakdown in $Q$ -learning. Further, the max operation implicit in the policy improvement serves to pick out the highest misestimated $Q$ -values such that $Q$ -values become extremely overestimated, often increasing unboundedly over training (Kumar et al., 2019; Levine et al., 2020). Offline Model-Based RL Model-based methods (Sutton, 1991) aim to solve the out-of-sample issue by allowing the agent to collect additional synthetic data in a learned dynamics model $\widehat{M} = (\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\widehat{T},\widehat{R},\mu_0,\gamma)$ . $\widehat{T}(s'|s,a)$ and $\widehat{R}(s,a)$ denote the approximate transition and reward functions, and are commonly realized as a deep ensemble (Chua et al., 2018; Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017). Methods typically use the MBPO procedure (Janner et al., 2019) shown in Algorithm 1, with synthetic data sampled as short $k$ -step trajectories (termed rollouts) under the current policy, starting from states in the offline dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{offline}}$ . # 3. Related Work Overestimation bias in $Q$ -learning. $Q$ -learning is a popular basis for many off-policy RL algorithms, however, it has been shown to suffer from an overestimation bias even in the online case (van Hasselt et al., 2016). In online RL, Fujimoto et al. (2018) demonstrate taking the minimum over two independently trained $Q$ -functions to be an effective solution, and extending this to larger $Q$ -ensembles has been shown to be beneficial for further control of overestimation (Chen et al., 2021). An et al. (2021) similarly apply taking a minimum over a $Q$ -ensemble in model-free offline RL to mitigate the more extreme pathological value overestimation caused by the out-of-sample problem. Offline Model-Free Methods Model-free offline algorithms can broadly be divided into action constraint methods and value pessimism-based methods, which each represent a different approach to the out-of-sample problem. Action constraint methods (Fujimoto & Gu, 2021; Kostrikov et al., 2022; Kumar et al., 2019) aim to avoid using out-of-sample actions in the Bellman update by ensuring selected actions are close to the dataset behavior policy $\pi^{\beta}$ . By contrast, value pessimism-based methods aim to directly regularize the value function such that it produces low-value estimates for out-of-sample state-action (An et al., 2021; Kostrikov et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2020), hence mitigating the overestimation mechanism described in Section 2. Of these, the most similar to our RAVL algorithm is EDAC (An et al., 2021) which applies value pessimism at any out-of-sample state-action using minimization over a $Q$ -ensemble. $^4$ Offline Model-Based Methods As alluded to in Section 1, the prevailing (incorrect) view in the offline model-based literature is that the ability to collect additional data in the model effectively resolves the out-of-sample issue, as the agent is now able to try out any previously out-of-sample behavior. The primary concern stated for model-based methods is therefore to account for errors in the learned dynamics model to avoid model exploitation. A broad class of methods explicitly penalizes the reward by the estimated level of model uncertainty (Ball et al., 2021; Kidambi et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2020), typically using variance over a dynamics ensemble. Rigter et al. (2022) aim to avoid model exploitation by setting up an adversarial two-player game between the policy and model. Critically, all previously described methods draw their motivation from dealing with dynamics model errors. Finally, most related to our method, COMBO (Yu et al., 2021), penalizes value estimates for state-action outside model rollouts. However, similarly to Yu et al. (2020), COMBO is theoretically motivated by the assumption of infinite horizon model rollouts, which we later show overlooks serious implications. # 4. The Edge-of-Reach Problem In the following section, we describe the central insight of our paper: the edge-of-reach problem. We begin by presenting the surprising result which exposes an error in current understanding. Next, we present our hypothesis, including intuition, empirical evidence on the main D4RL benchmark (Fu et al., 2020), and theoretical proof of its effect on offline model-based training. # 4.1. Surprising Result: Failure with the True Dynamics As described in Section 1, the current understanding in offline model-based RL is that, by adding a model to enable the collection of new data throughout training, the offline problem is effectively transformed into online learning. With this view, the key remaining difference compared to online RL is that: in online RL, data is collected with the true dynamics, while in offline model-based RL, data is collected in an approximate dynamics model. Existing model-based algorithms use this understanding, and as a result base their approaches on trying to mitigate the effect of dynamics model errors, for example by introducing reward or termination penalties based on estimates of dynamics uncertainty (Kidambi et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2020). This understanding naturally leads to the belief that the ideal case would be to have a perfect model with zero dynamics error. In Table 1, however, we show that this is surprisingly not the case. Instead, when the learned dynamics model (Learned) is replaced with the true dynamics (Oracle), the agent fails to train at all in most environments.5 This re ![](images/01aabad9457c1e2c73b3e7558371062312f99d559ea20d52094161050834072b.jpg) Figure 2: An illustration of how states that are sampled only in the final step of rollouts (i.e. as $s_k$ ) will appear only as nextstates in the model-based training distribution. These states will be used as targets in the Bellman update (see Equation (1)), but will not appear as $s$ in the dataset, and hence never themselves be updated. This mismatch leads to a breakdown of Bellman-based learning. sult is significant as it indicates the failure of all existing dynamics-penalized methods since all dynamics-penalized algorithms (Kidambi et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2020) collapse to exactly the same process under the Oracle (due to all sharing the same MBPO procedure (Algorithm 1) and all basing their penalties on dynamics uncertainty (ostensibly to address model errors) which will be zero since the Oracle has no uncertainty). This prompts our subsequent investigation, in which we reveal that offline model-based methods suffer from a previously unnoticed edge-of-reach problem. In Section 7.4, we discuss why these prior methods work (with a learned model) despite this critical oversight. # 4.2. The Edge-Of-Reach Hypothesis Our observation in Section 4.1 reveals that issues in offline model-based RL cannot be explained by dynamics model errors - a widespread misconception. We therefore require a different understanding. We begin with the main intuition: in offline model-based RL, synthetic data $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{rollouts}}$ is generated as short $k$ -step rollouts starting from states in the original dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{offline}}$ (see Algorithm 1). Crucially, under this procedure, there can exist some edge-of-reach states which can be reached in the final rollout step, but which cannot - under any policy - be reached earlier (see Figure 1 red). Sampling these states triggers a breakdown in learning, since even with the ability to collect unlimited additional data, the agent is never able to reach them 'in time' to try actions from them and hence never receives feedback. More concretely: Figure 2 illustrates how, due to being sampled only at the final step in a rollout, edge-of-reach states will be used for targets in Bellman-based learning but are never themselves updated. Thus, the out-of-sample action problem in model-free methods persists: since values at edge-of-reach states can be arbitrarily misestimated, incorrect values are then propagated over the entire state-action space. Moreover, when used with function approximation, the max operation in policy improvement can then exploit this misestimation, picking out the most heavily overesti mated values (Levine et al., 2020). This results in extreme value overestimation, often with $Q$ -values increasing unboundedly over training (as we see in Figure 3). # Edge-of-Reach Hypothesis: The procedure of limited horizon rollouts from a fixed dataset leads to the existence of edge-of-reach states at which the agent is unable to collect corrective feedback. This lack of corrective feedback triggers pathological value overestimation. Do we expect this to actually happen in practice? Failure via this mode requires $(a)$ existence of edge-of-reach states, and $(b)$ such edge-of-reach states to be sampled. The typical combination of $k << H$ along with a limited pool of starting states $(s \in \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{offline}})$ means the rollout distribution is unlikely to sufficiently cover the full state space $S$ , making $(a)$ likely. Moreover, we observe pathological 'edge-of-reach seeking' behavior in which the agent appears to 'seek out' edge-of-reach states due to this being the source of overestimation (see Section 5), thus making $(b)$ likely. In Appendix A, we give a more thorough and unified view of model-free and model-based offline RL, dividing the problem into independent conditions for states and actions. # 4.3. Definitions and Formalization We now formalize the intuitions presented in Section 4.2, and present theoretical grounding for the edge-of-reach problem and how errors can propagate to all transitions. Definition 1 (Edge-of-reach states). Consider a deterministic transition model $T: S \times \mathcal{A} \to S$ , rollout length $k$ , and some distribution over starting states $\nu_0$ . For some policy $\pi: S \to \mathcal{A}$ , rollouts are then generated according to $s_0 \sim \nu_0(\cdot)$ , $a_t \sim \pi(\cdot | s_t)$ and $s_{t+1} \sim T(\cdot | s_t, a_t)$ for $t = 0, \ldots, k-1$ , giving $(s_0, a_0, s_1, \ldots, s_k)$ . Let us use $\rho_{t,\pi}(s)$ to denote the marginal distributions over $s_t$ . We define a state $s \in S$ edge-of-reach with respect to $(T, k, \nu_0)$ if: for $t = k$ , $\exists \pi$ s.t. $\rho_{t,\pi}(s) > 0$ , but, for $t = 1, \ldots, k - 1$ and $\forall \pi$ , $\rho_{t,\pi}(s) = 0$ . In our case, $\nu_{0}$ is the distribution of states in $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{offline}}$ . With stochastic transition models (e.g. Gaussian models), we may have the case that no state will truly have zero density, and we relax this definition slightly to $\rho_{t,\pi}(s) < \epsilon$ for some small $\epsilon$ . The next proposition quantifies how errors in edge-of-reach states are propagated to preceding states. Proposition 1 (Error propagation from edge-of-reach states). Consider a rollout of length $k$ , $(s_0, a_0, s_1, \ldots, s_k)$ . Suppose that the state $s_k$ is edge-of-reach and the approximate value function $Q^j(s_k, \pi(s_k))$ has error $\epsilon$ . Then, standard value iteration will compound error $\gamma^{k-t} \epsilon$ to the estimates of $Q^{j+1}(s_t, a_t)$ for $t = 1, \ldots, k-1$ . (Proof in Appendix D.) In the next section, we provide further evidence of this edge-of-reach problem being the predominant issue in offline model-based RL. # 4.4. Evidence for the Edge-of-Reach Problem There are two potential issues in offline model-based RL: (1) dynamics model errors and subsequent model exploitation, and (2) the edge-of-reach problem and subsequent pathological value overestimation. We ask: Which is the true source of the issues observed in practice? While (1) is stated as the sole issue and hence the motivation in prior methods, the results in Table 1 are strongly at odds with this explanation. Furthermore, in Table 2 we check and find that the difference between the rewards predicted by the model vs the true rewards is insignificant, which means that (1) fails to explain the value explosion in Figure 3. Instead, edge-of-reach-induced pathological overestimation mechanism of (2) exactly predicts this value explosion, with the observations very closely resembling those of the analogous model-free out-of-sample problem (Kumar et al., 2019). Analysis with a Simple Environment In the previous section, we provided a plausible theoretical explanation and intuition for unexpected failure observed in Section 4.1. In this section, we construct a simple environment and use careful analysis to empirically confirm this hypothesis. We first show that naive application of actor-critic algorithms results in exploding $Q$ -values and failure to learn despite using the true dynamics model. Next, we verify that edge-of-reach states are the source of this problem by showing that correcting value estimates only at these states is sufficient to resolve the problem. # 5.1. Setup We construct a simple environment to allow us to investigate a distilled version of the edge-of-reach problem. We define reward as exponentially decreasing away from a fixed goal as shown in Figure 4(a), a simple deterministic transition function of $\mathbf{s}^* = \mathbf{s} + \mathbf{a}$ , where $\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}\in \mathbb{R}^2$ and horizon $H = 30$ . Initial states (analogous to $s\in \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{offline}}$ ) are sampled from the region shown in the blue box i.e. $\mu_0 = U([-2,2]^2)$ . We use SAC (Haarnoja et al., 2018) as the agent as in the standard offline model-based algorithms MOPO (Yu et al., 2020) and MOBILE (Sun et al., 2023), and actions are bounded $\| \mathbf{a}\| _1\leq 1$ as standard. The only difference here compared to online RL is that we use a data collection horizon of $k = 10$ such that $k < H$ . This small change results in the existence of edge-of-reach states (those between the red and orange boxes in Figure 4), and hence captures the problematic component of the MBPO procedure (see Algorithm 1). The procedure is therefore training SAC in the true environment with limited length trajectories, exactly as is done in Experiment 4.1. Note: There is no notion of an approximate dynamics model, as we are demonstrating that the issues are not caused by dynamics model errors, as is currently assumed. We instead demonstrate that it is the existence of edge-of-reach states (due to the use of $k < H$ as per the standard MBPO procedure) that triggers pathological value overestimation. # 5.2. Observing Pathological Value Overestimation Since the only difference between this setup and online RL is the use of trajectory collection horizon $k < H$ (as in MBPO), we may expect SAC to learn a sensible policy. However, we observe that SAC fails, with $Q$ -values growing unboundedly over training (see blue Figure 4(c,d)). Looking at the rollout trajectories sampled over training (see Figure 7) we see the following: (Before 25 epochs) Initially, the agent follows the reward function, and performance increases. (Between 25 and 160 epochs) Value misestimation takes over, and the policy begins to aim toward unobserved state-action (since their values can be misestimated and hence overestimated), and performance subsequently decreases. (After 160 epochs) This 'edge-of-reach seeking' behavior compounds with each epoch, leading to the agent eventually reaching edge-of-reach states. From this point onwards, the agent samples edge-of-reach states at which it never receives any corrective feedback. The consequent pathological value overestimation results in a complete collapse in performance. In Figure 4(b) we visualize the final policy and see that it completely ignores the reward function. Instead, it aims towards an arbitrary edge-of-reach state with the highest (heavily overestimated) $Q$ -value. # 5.3. Verifying the Hypothesis Using Value Patching Our hypothesis is that the source of this problem is value misestimation at edge-of-reach states. We verify this with our SAC-OraclePatch experiments, in which we replace a subset of the value estimates in the Bellman targets with their true values. In yellow in Figure 4 we demonstrate that applying patching solely for edge-of-reach states is sufficient to completely solve the problem. This is particularly compelling as in practice only a very small proportion of states had correct values patched in (0.4% of states over training). Of course, patching in true values is not possible in practice, thus in the next section we develop a practical approximation to this. We show in Section 7.1 that our proposed method, RAVL (see green in Figure 4), has a very similar effect to that of the ideal SAC-OraclePatch intervention and completely resolves the edge-of-reach problem. # 6. RAVL: Reach-Aware Value Learning As verified in Section 5.3, the edge-of-reach problem stems from value overestimation at edge-of-reach states. To resolve this issue, we therefore need to $(A)$ detect and $(B)$ prevent value overestimation at edge-of-reach states. (A) Detecting edge-of-reach states: As illustrated in Figure 2, edge-of-reach states are those that remain outside the distribution of states being updated, i.e. the outside training distribution of the $Q$ -function, $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{rollouts}}$ . A natural solution to detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs is to use a deep ensemble (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017). As such, high variance over an ensemble of $Q$ -functions can be used to detect edge-of-reach states. We demonstrate that this is effective in Figure 5. Note this is different to related model-free methods since the distribution being considered is that of $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{rollouts}}$ rather than $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{offline}}$ . (B) Preventing overestimation at these states: Once we have detected edge-of-reach states, we may simply apply value pessimism methods from the offline model-free literature to these states. Our choice of an ensemble for part (A) conveniently allows us to simply minimize over an ensemble of $Q$ -functions, which effectively penalizes values based on ensemble variance. Our resulting proposal is Reach-Aware Value Learning (RAVL). Concretely, RAVL simply involves training an ensemble of $N_{\text{critic}}$ $Q$ -functions similarly to EDAC (An et al., 2021), indexed by $n$ , and modifying Equation (1) to: $$ \begin{array}{l} Q _ {n} ^ {j + 1} \leftarrow \underset {Q _ {n}} {\arg \min } \mathbb {E} _ {(s, a, r, s ^ {\prime}) \sim \mathcal {D}, a ^ {\prime} \sim \pi^ {j} (\cdot | s ^ {\prime})} [ \\ \underbrace {\left(\underbrace {Q _ {n} (s , a)} _ {\text {i n p u t}}\right) - \left[ r + \gamma \min _ {n = 1 , \dots , N _ {\text {c r i t c}}} Q _ {n} ^ {j} \left(s ^ {\prime} , a ^ {\prime}\right)\right]}\left. \right) ^ {2} ] \tag {2} \\ \end{array} $$ As is standard in offline model-based RL, we optimize this objective using MBPO (Janner et al., 2019) and SAC (Haarnoja et al., 2018) as in Algorithm 1. RAVL is therefore a solution to offline model-based RL, which relies solely on value pessimism ideas from the model-free literature. This is in stark contrast to typical methods which use dynamics uncertainty penalization and therefore also provides further evidence that the edge-of-reach problem is the true source of issues. RAVL represents combining model-based training with the current SOTA model-free algorithm EDAC. The addition of the model compared to EDAC can be seen as relaxing the value pessimism requirements from any state-action OOD with respect to $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{offline}}$ , to those OOD with respect to $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{rollouts}}$ . This perspective highlights our algorithm's simplicity, with the approach being made possible due to our corrected understanding of the true issues involved in model-based offline RL. Our subsequently unified view of model-based and model-free approaches has allowed us to transfer ideas from the model-free literature for dealing with the out-of-sample problem and directly apply them to solve the edge-of-reach issue in the model-based setting. # 7. Empirical Evaluation In this section, we first evaluate RAVL on the simple environment from Section 5. Next, we show that RAVL scales, achieving strong performance on the standard D4RL benchmark and a new state-of-the-art on challenging pixel-based V-D4RL tasks. Finally, we compare RAVL to prior dynamics uncertainty penalized methods and elucidate why they may work despite not explicitly addressing the edge-of-reach problem. We provide full hyperparameters and a discussion of run-time in Appendix C.2. # 7.1. Evaluation on the Simple Environment We first test RAVL on the simple environment from Section 5 (see green in Figure 4). We observe that it achieves the same result as the theoretically optimal but practically impossible method of patching in the true values at edge-of-reach states, SAC-OraclePatch. The $Q$ -values are stabilized and match those of SAC-OraclePatch. Moreover, in Figure 5, we demonstrate that RAVL can precisely detect edge-of-reach states as they have significantly higher ensemble variance than within-reach states, as expected. # 7.2. Evaluation on the D4RL Benchmark Next, we show that RAVL scales to the standard offline RL benchmark, D4RL (Fu et al., 2020). We consider the MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012) v2 datasets. Figure 3 shows RAVL successfully stabilizes training, and Table 3 shows that we can match the performance of the current top model-based method, MOBILE (Sun et al., 2023), without the need for any explicit dynamics penalization. Evaluation on Pixel-Based tasks The insights from RAVL also lead to improvements in performance on the challenging pixel-based benchmark V-D4RL (Lu et al., 2023). This uses the Offline DreamerV2 algorithm which trains on trajectories in a learned latent space, thus demonstrating that the edge-of-reach problem is more general and widespread. We observe in Table 4 that RAVL gives a strong boost in performance $(+20.3\%)$ overall) on the medium and medexp level datasets, while not helping in the more diverse random and mixed datasets. This observation fits with our intuition of the edge-of-reach problem: the medium and medexp level datasets are likely to have less coverage of the state space, and thus we would expect them to suffer more from edge-of-reach issues and the 'edge-of-reach seeking behavior' demonstrated in Section 5.2. Reinterpretation of Prior Methods Prior model-based methods were unaware of the edge-of-reach problem, instead being motivated solely by mitigating issues due to model errors. However, our investigation strongly suggests that the edge-of-reach problem is likely to be the true main underlying issue on the D4RL benchmark (see Section 4.4). This leads us to ask: What allows prior model error-motivated methods to work despite ignoring the critical edge-of-reach problem? We find that, while ostensibly to address model errors, existing dynamics penalties may accidentally help to address the edge-of-reach problem, as we observe a positive correlation between the penalties used in dynamics uncertainty methods and RAVL's effective penalty of value ensemble variance (see Figure 6 in Appendix B.1). This may be expected, as dynamics uncertainty will naturally be higher further away from $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{offline}}$ which is also where edge-of-reach states are more likely to lie. We additionally note that, since the edge-of-reach problem is orthogonal to dynamics misestimation, RAVL could be combined with appropriate model uncertainty penalization (Lu et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2020) for environments with less accurate models. # 8. Conclusion In this paper, we expose a major misunderstanding in current model-based offline RL. We provide strong evidence that - contrary to common understanding - the true source of issues experienced by current methods is the edge-of-reach problem, a previously unnoticed issue whereby the standard offline model-based RL procedure leads to the existence of a set of edge-of-reach states that triggers pathological value misestimation and collapse of learning. Exposing this reveals a strong connection between model-free and model-based offline RL, which allows us to unify our understanding of these two areas. Based on this new unified perspective, we are able to transfer ideas from model-free literature and directly apply them to solve the edge-of-reach problem in model-based methods. Our resulting practical algorithm RAVL, is simple, robust, and achieves strong performance across both proprioceptive and pixel-based benchmarks. We open-source our code and hope that the insights presented here may help further ideas to be transferred between model-free and model-based methods. Finally, a more complete theoretical picture could be obtained by transferring finite horizon rollout theory from online model-based reinforcement learning to the offline setting (Janner et al., 2019). # Statement of Broader Impact This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of offline reinforcement learning. Since we evaluate on simulated control problems in this paper, we do not expect any specific ethical concerns to arise. However, when offline reinforcement learning is deployed in the real world, it is important to follow responsible ethical principles in ensuring the trustworthiness and reliability of our systems. # Acknowledgements Anya Sims and Cong Lu are funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC).
